text: Operator splitting: Lie–Trotter and Strang Operator splitting advances separate parts of an evolution equation and composes their solution maps. Lie–Trotter uses two full substeps; Strang surrounds one full substep with two half substeps. Even exact subproblem solutions leave a composition error when their order matters. Run both on the same reaction–diffusion input: a 32-point, T=1 Schnakenberg system with matched initial fields, subsolvers and observation times. Four step sizes measure first-order Lie–Trotter and second-order Strang. Unsplit Radau/DOP853 references use the same FD semidiscretization; this is separate from spatial convergence and exact continuum solutions. Start with a sufficiently smooth autonomous finite-dimensional initial-value problem. Each φ is the exact flow of its subproblem, and h is one step for the summed equation. Compositions act from right to left. Advancing F for h and then G for h approximates one step of length h for the original equation, not 2h. Using only h/2 for each part would instead halve the leading vector field. The approach uses tractable subproblems such as reaction and diffusion, transport and sources, or drift and force in a separable Hamiltonian. Splitting is a separate choice from spatial discretization and physical modeling. Matrix exponentials below apply to the linear specialization F(u)=Au, G(u)=Bu. Expansion through the quadratic term cancels the leading Lie–Trotter defect, leaving local O(h³) and global O(h²) errors; nested commutators enter the next error terms. For commuting finite matrices, both exact-subflow compositions equal the exact summed flow. Extending this statement to unbounded PDE operators requires domain and regularity conditions. Conditions: order and stability can be lost The stated orders assume a smooth solution, sufficiently small steps, a fixed finite interval and suitable stability. Shocks, stiff relaxation and nonsmooth initial data can invalidate those expectations. PDE subproblems and their stages need compatible boundary data. Check order reduction from inhomogeneous or time-dependent boundaries separately from spatial and nonlinear-solver errors. A symmetric arrangement alone does not make approximate subflows second order. Standard Strang composition needs subsolvers with at least second-order consistency and sufficiently tight iteration tolerances to retain second order. Exact or symmetric subsolvers are needed to retain time symmetry as well. Direct substitution of forward or backward Euler generally reduces the order to one. For this oscillator both update matrices have determinant 1 and trace 2−h², giving bounded oscillatory modes for 0<|h|<2. Exact subflows do not by themselves guarantee unconditional stability. Composition inherits only properties preserved by its submaps: Hamiltonian symplecticity does not imply positivity for arbitrary reactions or exact conservation of the full energy. Existing Strang examples and the distinction from IMEX The existing reaction–diffusion finite-amplitude Schnakenberg and saturated-pattern examples use exact half steps of centered-difference diffusion and a full implicit-midpoint reaction step in a Strang composition. Their published records give spatial and temporal checks for those fixed conditions. They are separate from this oscillator illustration, and their distributions, tolerances and results are preserved. IMEX also separates parts of the right-hand side, but IMEX time integration combines explicit and implicit stage equations, whereas the splitting here composes subproblem flows. These are different updates. For the separable-Hamiltonian connection, see symplectic integration.
